title: Cestrum parqui

{{Short description|Species of flowering plant}} {{Speciesbox |image = Cestrum parqui (8704387661).jpg |genus = Cestrum |species = parqui |authority = [[L'Hér.]] }} '''''Cestrum parqui''''', commonly known as '''palqui''', '''green cestrum''', '''Chilean cestrum''', '''green poisonberry''', or '''willow-leaved jessamine''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] native to [[Chile]]. In cultivation in the [[United Kingdom]] this plant has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/3458/i-Cestrum-parqui-i/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Cestrum parqui'' | accessdate=12 January 2018}} (confirmed 2017).{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 16 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 24 January 2018}} In [[Australia]], the plant is regarded as an [[Invasive species in Australia|invasive species]]. ==Description== ''C. parqui'' is a fast-growing, straggling, woody, [[semi-evergreen]] shrub that grows to over 3 metres in height (or more in warmer areas) with one or a few fragile green stems. Leaves are alternate, light green in colour, [[lance]]-shaped or marginally [[elliptic]] (that are wide at the middle), narrowly tapered at both ends, mainly 30–65 mm long and 8–23 mm wide. They have an unpleasant rubber-like smell when crushed. In areas with cool winters, the plant is partly deciduous. ===Inflorescences=== It produces terminal sprays of small, pungent-scented,[https://as.vanderbilt.edu/clacx/garden/plant-database/cestrum-parqui/ Cestrum parqui] Vanderbilt University. Retrieved 24 November 2022. tubular yellow-green flowers 2.5 cm long, followed by bunches of small, black, egg-shaped [[berries]] produced from summer to autumn. All parts of the plant are reported to be highly toxic.{{cite web | url = https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/cestrum_parqui.htm | title = Weeds of Australia: Biosecurity Queensland Edition | publisher = Queensland Government | accessdate = 28 August 2018}} Whilst the flower colors are generally yellow-green, some varieties have [[Saffron (color)|mustard orange]], creamy white, golden yellow and [[International orange|reddish-orange]] colors.[https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/cestrum/ Cestrum] [[NC State University]]. Retrieved February 2, 2025. The flowers have an unpleasant odor during the day, but are fragrant (sweet-scented) at night.{{cite web | url = https://www.business.qld.gov.au/industries/farms-fishing-forestry/agriculture/biosecurity/plants/invasive/other/green-cestrum | title = Green cestrum| publisher = Queensland Government | accessdate = 21 December 2023}}{{cite web | url = https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/weeds/weeds-information/chilean-cestrum | title = Chilean cestrum| publisher = [[Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action]] | accessdate = 21 December 2023}}{{cite web | url = https://sydneyweeds.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/Weed-Fact-Sheet-Green-Cestrum.pdf | title = Green Cestrum Cestrum parqui| publisher = Sydney Weeds Committees | accessdate = 21 December 2023}} The plant [[Free-flowering|flowers throughout the year]] (particularly in warmer climates), more so from spring to autumn, but the blooming is more prolific during spring.{{cite web | url = https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/cestrum_parqui.htm#:~:text=Flowering%20occurs%20throughout%20the%20year,purplish%2Dblack%20as%20they%20mature. | title = Cestrum parqui L'Hér.| publisher = Environmental Weeds of Australia | accessdate = 22 December 2023}} The small, black fruits of ''Cestrum parqui'' are highly attractive to birds, which play a major role in [[seed dispersal]], passing the seeds in their droppings: [[seedling]]s are thus often found growing under perching trees, along fencelines, and in creek banks, where it is also dispersed by water. ==Uses== ===Medicinal=== The plant contains toxic [[alkaloid]]s. It has been used in [[folk medicine]] to treat tumours and [[haemorrhoids]] and possesses sudorific ([[perspiration]]-inducing), [[laxative]] and [[antispasmodic]] properties. Decoctions or infusions of the plant have also been administered in cases of [[intermittent fever]] and an infusion of the inner bark drunk to treat unspecified "stomach ailments". [[File:Cestrum parqui leaf NC1.jpg|220px|thumb|Stem and leaves of C. parqui]] A [[poultice]] prepared from the plant (part unspecified) in combination with ''[[Solanum nigrum]]'' (part unspecified) and the crushed stems of ''[[Vitis vinifera]]'', the grape vine, is believed in folk medicine to have anti-inflammatory properties.Quattrocchi, Umberto (2012). CRC World dictionary of medicinal and poisonous plants: common names, scientific names, eponyms, synonyms and etymology, pub. CRC Press Taylor and Francis Group. Vol. II C-D, page 201. A crude extract of its aerial parts in [[methanol]] water displayed inhibition of [[carrageenin]]-induced [[oedema]].{{cite journal | pmid=10441792 | year=1999 | last1=Shehnaz | first1=D. | last2=Hamid | first2=F. | last3=Baqai | first3=F. T. | last4=Uddin Ahmad | first4=V. | title=Effect of the crude extract of Cestrum parqui on carrageenin-induced rat paw oedema and aggregation of human blood platelets | journal=Phytotherapy Research | volume=13 | issue=5 | pages=445–447 | doi=10.1002/(sici)1099-1573(199908/09)13:5<445::aid-ptr477>3.0.co;2-w | s2cid=22899396 }} ===Tobacco substitute=== Carl Hartwich, in his monumental work of 1911 on recreational drugs ''Die Menschlichen Genussmittel...'' ('The Pleasure Drugs of Humankind...'), records the following:
On the island of [[Chiloe Archipelago|Chiloe]], when there is a lack of [[tobacco]], the Cholos Indians replace it with another Solanacea ''Palguin'' or ''Palquin'', which they apparently smoked before the first [i.e. tobacco derived from various [[Nicotiana]] species] became known. The plant, ''Cestrum parqui L'Her.'', a small tree with lanceolate leaves and yellowish-white flowers, appears to be widespread in South America, it is found throughout Chile and the southern states of Brazil. In Chile they say of a well-known person: 'He is as famous as ''Palqui''{{'}}. The leaves (which are toxic to cattle) and the wood are used medicinally. I was able to detect a trace of alkaloid in the latter. [translated from the original German]Hartwich, Carl, ''Die Menschlichen Genussmittel, ihre herkunft, verbreitung, geschichte, anwendung, bestandteile und wirkung'' (Translation: ''The Pleasure-drugs of Mankind – their origins, spread, history, application, ingredients and effects''), pub. Leipzig 1911 Chr. Herm. Tauchnitz. Page 523 under heading 4: 'Cestrum parqui L'Her.'.
===Ritualistic=== Branches of ''Cestrum parqui'' are used to slap patients during [[Machi (shaman)|shamanic]] healing ceremonies that utilize the hallucinogenic and [[anticholinergic]] plant ''[[Latua pubiflora]]'', which are performed by the indigenous [[Huilliche]] people of the [[Los Lagos Region]] of southern [[Chile]]. This is due to the belief that the foul smell of the ''Cestrum'' plant is abhorrent to the demons believed to be causing the patient's illness and will cause them to leave the patient's body via [[vomiting]].Plowman, Timothy, Gyllenhaal, Lars Olof and Lindgren, Jan Erik ''Latua pubiflora'' magic plant from southern Chile ''Botanical Museum Leaflets Harvard University'' Vol. 23, No. 2, Cambridge, Massachusetts, November 12, 1971. ==Invasiveness== [[File:Cestrum parqui plant NC2.jpg|thumb|220px|Plant growing as a weed near [[Newcastle, New South Wales|Newcastle]], Southeastern Australia]] Because of its easy dispersal, it is considered to be a [[noxious weed]] in Australia, where it is even prohibited for merchandising in [[New South Wales]], as it is a significant hazard to [[livestock]] (especially cattle) which may eat it inadvertently or during shortages of other foods, often resulting in death.[https://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/Weeds/GreenCestrum Green cestrum (Cestrum parqui)] by NSW WeedWise Although it is no longer a fashionable [[garden plant]] and is now a [[garden escape]], it may still be found in old gardens.[https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/cestrum_parqui.htm Cestrum parqui L’Hér.] Environmental Weeds. Retrieved 31 December 2023. It was introduced as an [[ornamental plant]] and was naturalized in Australia in the 1920s, where it was recorded in the [[Brisbane Botanic Gardens, Mount Coot-tha|Brisbane Botanic Gardens]] in 1924 and naturalised at [[Ashgrove, Queensland|Ashgrove]] in 1926. By 1928, the species was blamed for livestock deaths in Brisbane's southern suburbs. Therefore, in 1933, it was declared a noxious weed in Queensland, whilst simultaneously becoming established in New South Wales. Cattle fatalities continued in the states of QLD and NSW throughout the 1940s and 1950s. It became naturalized in [[Victoria (state)|Victoria]] in the early 1940s, where it was observed in the [[Yarra Ranges National Park|Yarra]] and [[Dandenong Ranges]] in 1980, although the species is relatively rare in that state.[https://weeds.org.au/profiles/green-poisonberry-cestrum/ Green Poisonberry, Green Cestrum, Chilean Cestrum, Black Nightshade, Chilean Cestrum, Willow Leaved Jessamine] Weeds Australia. Retrieved 21 December 2023.[https://weedsofmelbourne.org/green-cestrum-cestrum-parqui Green Cestrum (Cestrum parqui)] Weeds of Melbourne.
